short_description: Repairing leading-edge erosion, coating damage and structural defects on installed wind turbine blades.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Robotic systems have demonstrated field repair and coating workflows, and Aerones and Rope Robotics sell leading-edge protection commercially, but deployments remain limited and most structural repair still depends on human rope-access teams. Paid work is concentrated in a few vendors and a few asset owners, which is the signature of a pilot market, not an early-commercial one.
advance_criteria: Repeated paid deployments across seasons, not one-off campaigns
Multiple asset owners, not one pilot partner
Demonstrated repair quality accepted by OEM warranty terms
Reduced on-site human intervention per blade
regress_criteria: A leading vendor exits or pivots to inspection only

evidence_considered.sentence: Rope Robotics targets task Blade repair

incumbent_process.text: Rope-access technicians or suspended platforms, with turbine downtime for every intervention and weather-limited working windows.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Rope access is the default across onshore and offshore fleets; platform access is used for larger repairs. Both stop the turbine and both are gated by wind speed and daylight.
advance_criteria: Would change if platform-free repair became the default for a fleet operator.

approaches.short_description: A robot lowered from the nacelle on ropes or cables and positioned against the blade for cleaning, coating, testing and repair.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Aerones and Rope Robotics sell suspended-robot cleaning, leading-edge protection and lightning-protection testing commercially to multiple owners; structural repair from the same platforms is still in pilot. Early commercial for the approach overall, with the caveat that repair specifically is a step behind.
advance_criteria: Structural repair sold as a standard service, not a trial
Fleets operating in more than one continent per vendor
Multi-year service agreements that name robotic maintenance

approaches.short_description: A robot that adheres to and walks along the blade surface, carrying inspection or repair tooling directly to the defect.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: BladeBUG-type crawlers have completed offshore trials and demonstrated inspection and light repair on live turbines, but there is no repeated paid deployment programme and deployment to the blade still needs a crew at the nacelle. The approach has the best contact geometry and the worst logistics.
advance_criteria: Paid campaigns across multiple wind farms in a season
Deployment without rope-access crew involvement
Repair quality accepted by an OEM or ISP under contract

approaches.short_description: A multirotor carrying an arm or tool that performs contact work on the blade while hovering.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Contact-stable manipulation from a multirotor at height in gusting wind is an open research problem; laboratory and short field demonstrations exist, commercial vendors do not. It stays on the board because it is the only approach that removes the nacelle crew entirely.
advance_criteria: Field demonstration of sustained contact work on a live turbine in measured wind
A vendor with a productised system and a paying pilot customer
Regulatory pathway for tethered or untethered contact flight near turbines

approaches.short_description: Multirotor drones flying close to blades for inspection; contact work from the same platform is early.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: For inspection the drone approach is mature and fleet-wide; for contact work such as cleaning or coating it is early. Rated as scaling for the approach as a whole because the inspection business funds the contact experiments and the same vendors sell both.
advance_criteria: Contact tasks (cleaning, coating) sold commercially from a drone platform
Autonomous, operator-free inspection flights as the default
BVLOS approvals for fleet campaigns in major markets

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: A repair is a multi-step process (clean, sand, fill, cure, coat) with process-quality requirements that warranties depend on.
advance_criteria: Would be relaxed if OEMs accepted protective tapes applied without surface prep.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Grinding, filling and coating all require a stable tool-to-surface contact while gusts load the platform; this is the physical constraint that separates inspection from repair.
advance_criteria: Drops out only if turbines are routinely stopped and locked for every repair.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Every approach has to solve deployment to and retrieval from the blade at hub height, which drives system mass, tether design and crew size.
advance_criteria: Fixed for the installed fleet.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: The robot must find and track the leading edge to millimetre precision on a curved, uniformly coloured surface, in varying light.
advance_criteria: Would be simplified by blade-embedded fiducials, which no OEM ships today.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: OEMs hold long-term service agreements on much of the installed base and control warranty acceptance of repair methods.
advance_criteria: Would change if owners moved service in-house at scale.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: ISPs compete on cost per blade and are the most likely early adopters of robots that cut crew size.
advance_criteria: Would change if ISP consolidation removed the cost-competition dynamic.

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Owners pay for downtime and are the ultimate sponsor of any method that shortens repair campaigns.
advance_criteria: Stable.

blockers.text: Warranty acceptance of robot-applied repairs by turbine OEMs

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: A repair nobody will warrant is a demo. OEM service terms still assume certified technicians, so robot repairs are confined to owner-operated fleets and out-of-warranty assets.
advance_criteria: An OEM publishes an approved robotic repair procedure
Insurers price robot-repaired blades the same as technician-repaired ones
ISPs win service contracts on the basis of robotic repair capacity

blockers.text: Weather windows and mobilisation cost still dominate campaign economics

assessment.author: editorial
assessment.rationale: Robots reduce crew hours on the blade but not the days lost to wind and rain, and mobilising a suspended system still needs a crew at the nacelle. Until the system works in higher wind than a technician can, the economic gain is capped.
advance_criteria: Demonstrated operation above the rope-access wind limit
Single-visit multi-blade campaigns without re-rigging
Published cost-per-blade below the ISP benchmark
